content.title: Did the astronauts who went to the moon get paid more, like maybe a bonus, than just the regular astronauts?
content.text: I’m always interested by how often this question comes up. As if the Apollo astronauts were just some contractors hired off the street to go to the Moon. They were all US government employees, before and after their mission. Neil Armstrong was a civilian, a civil servant Federal government employee working for NASA, as he had been since 1955. He joined NASA after leaving the Navy - he had been a fighter pilot in the Korean War - and became a test pilot for the Agency, flying the X-15 rocket plane. As a fairly senior civil servant, he made about $27,000 annually, roughly $190,000 in current dollars. Collins and Aldrin were both active duty lieutenant colonels in the US Air Force, and made the equivalent of about $140,000 a year in current dollars. They did file travel claims once they got back to Houston, for $33.31 in per diem.Q: Did the astronauts who went to the moon get paid more, like maybe a bonus, than just the regular astronauts? IIRC, they got flight pay, and some small latitude on expenses, but no specific bonus. There was a small per-diem (< $10 per day). No hazard pay. I think I remember one of them (Jack Swigert, Jeremy Lowe tells me in the comments, thanks) forgot to do his tax return, and had the IRS penalty waived by Presidential order. I’m not sure if hazard pay can be granted retroactively, but if so, I think the crew of Apollo 13 could have made a fairly convincing case.Q: How much money did Neil Armstrong and "Buzz" Aldrin earn for their 1 1/2 hour trek on the moon? Did they get a bonus or just their regular salary?Apollo astronauts received an $8 per diem in addition to their salary (about $17,000 in most cases, or about $112,000 today). That works out to fifty cents each for the EVA—the cost of a good cup of coffee. The astronauts could not get insurance (and could not have afforded it) so they spent their confinement in the days before launch signing hundreds of autographs so their families would have a source of income in the event anything went wrong.Yes — Apollo astronauts who flew to the Moon received higher pay than career Air Force/Navy/astronaut-office base pay alone, but not large commercial-style bonuses. Their compensation came from a combination of military pay (for military astronauts), civil-service pay (for civilian astronauts), special pay differentials, and modest flight or hazardous-duty allowances. Key points:Base pay depended on rank and employment status:Military astronauts continued to receive their regular military pay and allowances (rank-based salary, housing, subsistence).Civilian NASA astronauts were paid on the federal General Schedule (GS) scale or equivalent SES-like levels.Special pay and differentials:NASA historically paid “flight pay” or “hazardous duty pay” to astronauts and some test pilots; amounts varied by era and individual status.During the Apollo era and afterward, astronauts received extra pay when ordered to flight status or for specific hazardous assignments. These differentials were modest compared with civilian salaries — typically a few hundred to a few thousand dollars per year in period dollars.No large mission-specific bonuses:There were no public records of multimillion-dollar bonuses tied specifically to lunar missions. Payment was structured through existing federal/military pay systems and mission assignments rather than commercial incentive bonuses.Astronauts did receive other non-pay compensation: high-profile status, career advancement, book/movie deals after returning to civilian life (separate from NASA pay), and government pensions. Some later-era astronauts negotiated paid consulting, speaking fees, or commercial opportunities after their missions.Examples and scale:Apollo-era pay differentials were small relative to the risks and prestige. Contemporary accounts cite modest hazardous-duty or flight pay increments; an Apollo astronaut’s total annual federal/military compensation in late 1960s–early 1970s usually remained within typical officer pay bands, not dramatically higher because of a Moon flight.In later programs (Space Shuttle era) similar rules applied: pay via government scales plus limited additional differentials, not mission bonuses.Modern private-sector contrast:Today, private commercial astronaut arrangements (space tourists or employees of private space companies) can include significantly different compensation structures, including larger performance bonuses, equity, or profit-sharing, depending on employer contracts.Summary: Moon-flying astronauts received higher overall compensation only insofar as their military rank/civil-service grade, flight/hazard pay, and post-flight commercial opportunities increased their income. There were no outsized NASA-paid “Moon mission bonuses” in the public record; extra pay was modest and administered through standard federal/military pay allowances.Just the regular paycheck, plus per diem for traveling away from home. Michael Collins was paid $17,147.76 as a lt. colonel in the Air Force, Buzz Aldrin pulled down $18,622.56 as a full colonel, and Neil Armstrong (as a civilian) was the highest paid astronaut in NASA - earning $27,401. Which was one the reasons some of the others resented him a bit. All 3 were eligible for per diem expenses for traveling away from home, for a grand total of 8 bucks a day per astronaut. I don’t know if Neil filed, but Collins and Aldrin did - requesting reimbursement “For Travel and Expenses” and listing their itinerary as “FROM: Houston, TX. TO: Cape Kennedy, FL… Moon… Pacific Ocean… USN Hornet… Hawaii… and returning to Houston TX.” Mode Of Travel: “Government Air”. Amount Requested: $33.31. Their requests were approved a month later.Some people today think they submitted per diem as a bit of a joke, but the fact is, they had families to feed. Even in 1969, 18 grand a year didn’t go far. It’s also worth noting that in addition to filing travel vouchers, they were required to fill out customs declaration forms. Because, after all - they’d traveled out of the country! Their itinerary was listed as “CAPE CANAVERAL - MOON - HONOLULU,” and they declared that they were bringing into the country “MOON ROCK AND MOON DUST SAMPLES.” To the question, “Any other condition onboard that may lead to the spread of disease”, the ominous answer was “TO BE DETERMINED…”I still think, though, that Wally Schirra topped them all. After his “Sigma 7” Mercury flight in 1962, “Jolly Wally” submitted a claim for mileage reimbursement for his 150,000 mile spaceflight. NASA responded by billing him for the Atlas rocket, which he had failed to return at the end of the mission. Both parties agreed to drop the matter and move on.Did the astronauts who went to the moon get paid more, like maybe a bonus, than just the regular astronauts? When I sat on the carpet in my living room glued to the black and white TV in 1969 and watch a human set foot on another body in the solar system I truly thought that by the year 2000 there would be such a thing as a “regular” astronaut. I was wrong. It is still an exceptional thing to be an astronaut.Difficult to answer. They weren’t passengers, but incredibly skilled and well-trained professionals risking their lives to do what had never been done before by anyone. You’d have to factor in the months or years of training *specifically* for this mission — and even risking their lives on Earth. For example, Armstrong could easily have died the time he had to bail out of the lunar lander during practice. More to your point — I don’t *think* they got anything beyond their salary, whatever that was. Remember also that NASA is a government entity, and the government has a pathological love for bureaucracy and paperwork. I heard Charlie Duke tell a story that he actually had to fill out a plain ordinary travel form, “Hmm… From: Cape Kennedy…. To: Moon…” etc. etc. Whereupon he asked, “Hey, do I get reimbursed for mileage?” With the response, “No, you’re taking our vehicle.” :)It is my understanding that the Apollo astronauts that went to the moon were paid an 8 dollar per diem for the days they were gone just as it were an official travel trip. They were not paid for accommodations because they were in a capsule/liner lander.Are NASA astronauts only paid between $80,000 and $140,000 per year? Considering the fact that they risk their lives, isn't that scanty? Or do they get any additional benefits?Astronaut pay? Hell yes, it's "scanty!" When compared to TV and movie stars; sports figures around the world; CEO’s of Fortune 500 companies and the like; astronauts don't get paid squat, even when one considers we do risk our lives. Yet most of us really don't care. We're doing what we've dreamed of doing, many of us since we were young children. My wife and I discuss this topic frequently. Our conversation always returns to the solid work of our United States military veterans. If we consider their “working conditions,” it puts those of astronauts in a different perspective. I cannot speak for my colleagues, but in my personal experience astronauts and military service men and women have similar experiences in some significant ways. We toil in the framework of government service, we are subjected to family separations, the result of long —and sometimes frequent— deployments. We must perform according to rules and regulations many would find overly restrictive. Yet we soldier on, many for our love of country and the impact we can have on people’s lives, including preserving freedom in America and around the world. But there is a big difference. As astronauts, we don’t put ourselves in harm’s way with the regularity of those defending our country abroad. I don’t recall many incidents where someone was shooting at me or my crewmates, or I was placed in the unenviable position of trying to find and avoid an IED. I never had to patrol a foreign land —wearing heavy (and hot) equipment that made my spacesuit look like a pair of overalls— protecting those who longed to live in freedom and not under some aggressively oppressive regime. Sure, I risked my life when I dove in the Neutral Buoyancy Lab during spacewalk training. Yes, I risked my life when I flew sorties in the T-38 jets to give me “spaceflight readiness training.” And of course I risked my life by jumping on an explosive-laden rocket to fly into the vacuum of outer space. But I did it infrequently, and all of those things were FUN! And when it was all over, people patted me on the back and told me how brave I was… how wonderfully I performed during the missions (well maybe not everyone…), and how cool they thought astronauts are. I never once worried about spending the rest of my life in a wheel chair, or fighting through years of rehabilitation without one of my arms or legs. I didn’t spend sleepless nights filled with horrible dreams and the effects of PTSD. Sure, it would be wonderful to be compensated like a Michael Jordan, or a Warren Buffett, but it’s not necessary for me. I was “living the dream.” Perhaps it's better that our brave military men and women receive more than the meager salaries they bring home now. And when they do return home? Thank them for their service and give them that pat on the back. They’re the ones that really earned it. Keep lookin’ up… and thanking our veterans!Ask a pro: "I'm 65 with $1M saved. What's my retirement budget?"This quiz matches nearly 50,000 people each month with vetted financial advisors.Buzz Aldrin filed his paperwork for travel expenses of $33.31 There was no special pay for actually going in to space etc. Neil Armstrong was on a higher pay scale than the other astronauts, but not because he went on a mission, or got to the moon. Buzz Aldrin’s was a Colonel in the Air Force, so his salary including fringe benefits was $18,622.56 a year. Michael Collins was a Lt. Colonel so was on $17,147.76 a year. So no bonus. But a lot of work, and a lot of risk.Astronauts are lucky they aren’t airline pilots… Otherwise they would have only gotten paid from the hatch was closed and they “pushed back” for launch (I guess that would be when they retracted the gantry.) until splash down. They would have gotten a lower rate for flying the LEM, and the time on the moon and the space walks would have been off the clock. I wonder what Virgin Galactic is gonna do? LOLDid the astronauts who went to the moon get paid more, like maybe a bonus, than just the regular astronauts? The “Bonus” was they went to the moon! Being one of 12 men in the whole world who have walked on the moon is the sort of “Bonus” that most people would kill for And if they DID want a financial return then there were plenty of opportunities to make a few extra bucks after they left NASADid Apollo 1 astronauts suffer?Define suffer. Yes, they knew there was a fire in capsule. No, they did not know how long they had. Based upon the medical telemetry data found in the NASA Blue Ribbon committee report, and other sources, the astronauts were deceased by heart failure in about 17 seconds but definitely less than 30 seconds. U.S. Air Force pathologists conducted examinations, concluding that the astronauts died of asphyxia from carbon monoxide and other toxic gases resulting from the fire. As for burn injuries, it was concluded that most of them had occurred postmortem. So, any answers indicating that they suffered from thermal burns are wrong, they were already dead. No one knows what high concentration, high pressure carbon monoxide respiratory infusion feels like. It is certainly not pleasant. RIP Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee. Let us never forget but let us all allow you a solemn eternity.
